claims.text: The initial AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles are smaller than 5 nm.
The nanoparticles were synthesized by pulsed laser deposition on a silicon nitride membrane.
The initial nanoparticles have elliptical or icosahedral geometries.
The initial nanoparticles exhibit a metastable FCC structure.
Au and Cu segregation is driven by surface-energy-minimization gradients.
Surface-energy gradients overcome the sluggish-diffusion barrier in the nanoparticles.
The observed segregation and particle loss are not caused by thermodynamic entropy stabilization.
High curvature at vertices and edges lowers the activation energy for surface diffusion.
Au and Cu are low-surface-energy elements in the relevant AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticle environment.
Curvature and element-specific surface-energy differences locally accelerate Au and Cu diffusion to the surface.
Surface enrichment by Au and Cu reduces the nanoparticles' total surface energy.
Au and Cu have sufficiently high vapor pressures at the relevant heating temperatures to evaporate preferentially.
Preferential Au and Cu evaporation causes nanoparticle shrinkage.
Surface-energy minimization causes the heated nanoparticles to reshape toward spherical geometries.
A critical temperature exists above which Au/Cu surface segregation and evaporation become faster than bulk diffusion.
Crossing the critical temperature causes rapid widening of the particle-size distribution.
Icosahedral particles have a lower critical temperature than truncated-octahedral particles because they have higher surface curvature and surface-energy density.
The proposed mechanism is valid only for nanoparticles smaller than 10 nm.
For particles larger than 20 nm, bulk sluggish diffusion dominates.
Particles larger than 20 nm retain an entropy-stabilized FCC structure without significant surface segregation or evaporation.
